title: Delhi Hospitals Treat 177 Diwali Burn Cases; Boy, 10, Dies in Narela Blast
excerpt: Safdarjung recorded 135 cases over two days and AIIMS 42 more, 11 of them serious. Most injuries were to the hands, and an eight-year-old with 45 per cent burns is in a serious condition.
body:
• Safdarjung Hospital in Delhi recorded 135 Diwali-related burn cases over November 7 and 8 — 129 from firecrackers and six from diyas — including 35 children treated as outpatients. Seven patients remained admitted on Monday.
  • AIIMS Delhi treated 42 more patients, 11 of them seriously injured and four in intensive care. An eight-year-old with burns over 45 per cent of the body is in a serious condition.
  • A 10-year-old boy died in Delhi's Narela area on Sunday night after a firecracker exploded in his hand, police said.
  • Most injuries were to the hands. The World Health Organization's burn first-aid guidance is to cool a burn under cool running water for about 20 minutes, never apply ice, oils or toothpaste, and seek urgent care for burns to the hands, face or large areas.

Delhi's two biggest burns units treated more than 177 people for Diwali-related burn injuries over the festival weekend, hospital officials said on Monday, and a 10-year-old boy died after a firecracker exploded in his hand.

Safdarjung: 135 cases in two days

Vardhman Mahavir Medical College and Safdarjung Hospital — home to one of the country's largest burns units — recorded 135 cases at its Burns Emergency Department over November 7 and 8, according to officials. Firecrackers caused 129 of them and diyas six. Thirty-five children with firecracker burns were treated on an outpatient basis, and one child required admission. The hospital had earmarked 20 beds for Diwali burn admissions; as of Monday, seven patients remained admitted. Reporting citing the hospital put the split at 93 men and 42 women, with 131 patients from Delhi and four from outside the capital.

The load is in line with last year, when Safdarjung recorded 129 burn cases over the two Diwali days — a comparison the hospital's own reporting cautions is not exact, because the counting windows differ. The pattern underneath the numbers is consistent, though: doctors noted that most injuries involved the hands, the predictable result of holding and lighting firecrackers directly.

AIIMS: 42 cases, 11 of them serious

AIIMS Delhi treated 42 patients, its Department of Plastic, Reconstructive and Burns Surgery said on Monday. Thirty-one had minor injuries and 11 had serious burns; four of the seriously injured are in the Intensive Care Unit and seven in general wards. Six children below the age of 10 were injured, among them an eight-year-old with burns across 45 per cent of the body whose condition is serious. Twelve patients were aged 10 to 18, and 22 were adults between 18 and 60. Five patients have undergone surgery, and eight remained admitted as of Monday. Of the 42 cases, 37 were caused by firecrackers and two by potash, including a 13-year-old, according to Dr Maneesh Singhal, who heads the department.

The Narela death

The weekend's worst outcome came from Narela, in north Delhi, where a 10-year-old boy died after a firecracker exploded in his hand while he was bursting crackers outside his home on the night of Sunday, November 8, according to police.

What to do if someone is burned

The WHO's burns fact sheet gives first aid that applies directly to firecracker injuries: cool the burn promptly under cool running water — about 20 minutes is commonly advised for smaller burns — remove rings and tight items early, and cover the burn with a clean, non-adherent dressing. Do not apply ice, oils, butter, toothpaste or traditional pastes. Burns to the hands or face, deep or large burns, and burns in young children need urgent medical care — the exact categories that filled Delhi's burns wards this weekend.
